chunks: He said: Ibrahim ibn al-Mustanir narrated from al-Mufaddal, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) say:

There are two occultations for the master of this affair; one of them being longer than the other, till it would be said: He has died; and some will say: He is killed. Thus only a few companions of the Imam would remain steadfast on his Imamate and no one would know about his whereabouts and his circumstances, except a servant, who would perform his errands.

key_terms.أَمْرِهِ: His affair/matter (referring to the Imamate and its management)
key_terms.الْمَوْلَى: The Servant/Deputy (specifically referring to the one who manages the Imam's affairs)
key_terms.صَاحِبُ الْأَمْرِ: The Master of the Affair (referring to the Imam of the Time)
key_terms.غَيْبَتَانِ: Two occultations (referring to the Minor and Major Ghaybah)

ai.seo_question: What are the two occultations of the Imam of the Time and how do people react to the longer one?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (a.s) establishes the theological foundation for the two occultations (al-Ghaybatan) of the Twelfth Imam, distinguishing between the Minor and Major Ghayba. It highlights the transition from a period of close contact with specific deputies to a prolonged era of general occultation where the Imam's location remains hidden from the public, known only to his ultimate deputy (al-Mawla al-Akbar). This concept is central to Shia eschatology, explaining the continuity of divine guidance despite the Imam's physical absence.
